thermal-properties-001.question: According to the Dulong–Petit law, the molar heat capacity of many solid elements near room temperature is about 3R (R is the gas constant, 8.31 J/(mol·K)). Estimating the specific heat per unit mass of aluminum (molar mass 26.98 g/mol) with this law, which value is closest?
choices: About 0.31 J/(g·K)
About 0.46 J/(g·K)
About 0.92 J/(g·K)
thermal-properties-001.explanation: Atoms in a solid vibrate in three directions, and the vibration in each direction holds kT/2 each as kinetic and potential energy, for a total of 3kT per atom, so the molar heat capacity is 3R ≈ 24.9 J/(mol·K). Dividing by the molar mass gives 24.9/26.98 ≈ 0.92 J/(g·K), close to the measured value for aluminum of about 0.90 J/(g·K). About 0.31 J/(g·K) drops the factor of 3 and divides R alone, and about 0.46 J/(g·K) uses (3/2)R, the constant-volume molar heat capacity of a monatomic gas, which leaves out the potential energy of the vibrations. Because the molar heat capacities are nearly the same, lighter elements have larger specific heats per unit mass.

thermal-properties-002.question: At temperatures well below the Debye temperature, how does the heat capacity of an insulating crystal (the lattice heat capacity) change with temperature?
choices: It stays nearly constant at 3R, regardless of the temperature
It decreases in proportion to the cube of the temperature
It decreases linearly, in direct proportion to the temperature
thermal-properties-002.explanation: The energy of lattice vibrations is quantized, and vibrations whose energy unit ħω is larger than kT are hardly excited. At temperatures well below the Debye temperature, only low-energy, long-wavelength acoustic phonons are excited, and their number grows with temperature, so the lattice heat capacity is proportional to T³ (the Debye T³ law). A nearly constant 3R is the classical limit at high temperatures comparable to or above the Debye temperature, corresponding to the Dulong–Petit law. A heat capacity proportional to temperature is the signature of the electronic heat capacity from conduction electrons in metals, which arises because only electrons near the Fermi level are thermally excited.

thermal-properties-003.question: Diamond is an electrical insulator, yet its thermal conductivity at room temperature is about 2000 W/(m·K), higher than that of copper (about 400 W/(m·K)). What is the main reason?
choices: Light carbon atoms with strong covalent bonds give a high sound speed, and the heat-carrying phonons are scattered little
The larger the band gap, the more conduction electrons are thermally excited, and these electrons carry the heat just as in metals
The crystal contains a great many freely moving holes, which carry most of the heat just as conduction electrons do in metals
thermal-properties-003.explanation: In an insulator, heat is carried mainly by phonons, the waves of lattice vibration. Thermal conductivity is expressed as a product of the heat capacity C, the speed of sound v and the mean free path l, as in κ = (1/3)Cvl. Because diamond has light atoms and strong bonds, its Debye temperature is high, about 1900–2200 K, its speed of sound is large, and at room temperature phonons rarely scatter off each other, so l is long. As a result it reaches about 2000 W/(m·K), exceeding the roughly 400 W/(m·K) of copper. With a band gap as large as about 5.5 eV, diamond has almost no thermally excited electrons or holes at room temperature, so they do not carry heat. In metals such as copper, most of the heat is carried by conduction electrons.

thermal-properties-004.question: Using the Wiedemann–Franz law κ = LσT (Lorenz number L = 2.44×10⁻⁸ W·Ω/K²), which value is closest to the estimated thermal conductivity of copper with an electrical conductivity σ = 5.9×10⁷ S/m at 300 K?
choices: About 430 W/(m·K)
About 39 W/(m·K)
About 1.4 W/(m·K)
thermal-properties-004.explanation: κ = 2.44×10⁻⁸×5.9×10⁷×300 ≈ 432 W/(m·K), about 430 W/(m·K). This is close to the measured value of about 400 W/(m·K), showing that conduction electrons carry most of the heat in metals. Electrons carry both charge and heat, and both are hindered by the same scattering, so κ/σ is proportional to the absolute temperature, with a proportionality constant, the Lorenz number, that is nearly the same for all metals. About 39 W/(m·K) uses the Celsius temperature of 27 instead of the absolute temperature. About 1.4 W/(m·K) forgets to multiply by the temperature. When alloying lowers the electrical conductivity, the thermal conductivity falls in nearly the same proportion.

thermal-properties-005.question: The thermal conductivity of pure copper at room temperature is about 400 W/(m·K), but in brass with about 30% zinc in solid solution it drops to about 120 W/(m·K). What is the main reason?
choices: Zinc hardly conducts heat, so the paths for heat are reduced by its volume
Solid solution softens the lattice and greatly lowers the speed of the phonons that carry most of the heat
Solute atoms scatter conduction electrons and shorten their mean free path, so the thermal conductivity falls along with the electrical conductivity
thermal-properties-005.explanation: Heat in metals is carried mainly by conduction electrons, so the thermal conductivity is nearly proportional to the electrical conductivity, the two being linked by the Wiedemann–Franz law. Zinc atoms in the copper lattice disturb the periodicity of the atomic arrangement and scatter electrons, shortening their mean free path, so the electrical conductivity of brass is only about 30% of that of pure copper. The thermal conductivity likewise falls from about 400 to about 120 W/(m·K). Zinc itself is a metal with a thermal conductivity of about 116 W/(m·K), not a substance that fails to conduct heat. In metals, phonons carry only part of the heat to begin with, so a small change in the lattice properties cannot explain such a large drop.

thermal-properties-006.question: The lattice thermal conductivity of an insulating single crystal decreases roughly in proportion to 1/T as temperature rises, at temperatures comparable to or above the Debye temperature. What is the main reason?
choices: Above the Debye temperature the heat capacity falls inversely with temperature, so phonons carry less heat
The number of phonons grows, and with it the phonon–phonon scattering that does not conserve total momentum (umklapp processes)
Thermal expansion of the lattice increases phonon scattering at crystal surfaces and grain boundaries, shortening the mean free path
thermal-properties-006.explanation: Among phonon collisions, normal processes, which conserve the total momentum, hardly impede the flow of heat, whereas umklapp processes, in which the total momentum changes by a reciprocal lattice vector, act against the heat flow and are the main source of thermal resistance. At high temperatures the number of phonons grows in proportion to temperature, so the mean free path shortens roughly as 1/T, and since the heat capacity is nearly constant, κ ∝ 1/T. Above the Debye temperature the heat capacity stays near 3R per mole of atoms; a sharp drop happens on the low-temperature side instead. Scattering at surfaces and grain boundaries hardly depends on temperature and dominates at very low temperatures, where the phonon mean free path is long; there κ falls with decreasing temperature, as the heat capacity does.

thermal-properties-007.question: For silicon (density 2330 kg/m³, specific heat 700 J/(kg·K)), take the room-temperature thermal conductivity as 150 W/(m·K) and the average phonon speed as 6000 m/s. Estimating the phonon mean free path l from κ = (1/3)Cvl, which has the same form as in the kinetic theory of gases (C is the heat capacity per unit volume), which value is closest?
choices: About 15 nm
About 5.1 nm
About 46 nm
thermal-properties-007.explanation: The heat capacity per unit volume is C = ρc = 2330×700 ≈ 1.63×10⁶ J/(m³·K). l = 3κ/(Cv) = 3×150/(1.63×10⁶×6000) ≈ 4.6×10⁻⁸ m, about 46 nm. About 15 nm drops the factor of 1/3 and uses κ/(Cv), and about 5.1 nm applies the 1/3 on the wrong side, giving κ/(3Cv). This estimate is an average that represents all phonons by a single speed and mean free path; in reality, low-frequency phonons with mean free paths of several hundred nm or more also carry much of the heat. For that reason, in silicon thin films and nanowires about 100 nm thick, surface scattering lowers the thermal conductivity well below the bulk value.

thermal-properties-008.question: Which value is closest to the thermal diffusivity α = κ/(ρc) of aluminum (thermal conductivity 237 W/(m·K), density 2700 kg/m³, specific heat 900 J/(kg·K))?
choices: About 9.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s
About 9.8×10⁻² m²/s
About 0.26 m²/s
thermal-properties-008.explanation: α = 237/(2700×900) = 237/(2.43×10⁶) ≈ 9.75×10⁻⁵ m²/s, about 9.8×10⁻⁵ m²/s. Thermal diffusivity expresses how quickly a change in temperature spreads through a material, and it appears in the transient heat conduction equation ∂T/∂t = α∇²T. A rough time for the temperature to change through a material of thickness L is L²/α, which for aluminum 10 mm thick is about 1 s. About 9.8×10⁻² m²/s uses the specific heat as 0.9 in J/(g·K), shifting the result by a factor of 1000. About 0.26 m²/s forgets to multiply by the density, giving κ/c, which does not even have units of m²/s.

thermal-properties-009.question: A metal plate and a wooden board are left long enough at the same room temperature (about 20°C). When touched by hand, the metal feels colder. What is the main reason?
choices: Metal's specific heat per unit mass far exceeds wood's, so it draws a lot of heat from the hand and stores it
Metal has a far larger effusivity √(κρc) than wood, so the contact surface ends up near the metal's temperature
Even at room temperature, heat escapes easily from the metal surface, so it is colder than the surface of the wood
thermal-properties-009.explanation: Right after two bodies at different temperatures touch, the temperature of the contact surface is an average weighted by their thermal effusivities e = √(κρc). Metal has a thermal conductivity hundreds of times or more that of wood and a far larger effusivity, so the contact surface drops to near 20°C, close to the metal's temperature, heat is drawn quickly from the skin, and the metal feels cold. With wood, the contact surface stays close to body temperature. Dry wood (about 1.7 J/(g·K)) actually has a larger specific heat per unit mass than aluminum (about 0.9 J/(g·K)), so specific heat cannot explain it. Left long enough at the same room temperature, both surfaces are at about room temperature, with no difference.

thermal-properties-010.question: In the laser flash method, a pulse of light was applied to the front of a disk of thickness L = 2.0 mm, and the time for the temperature rise of the back face to reach half its maximum was t½ = 0.050 s. Which value is closest to the thermal diffusivity found with Parker's equation α = 0.1388L²/t½, which neglects heat loss?
choices: About 8.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s
About 1.1×10⁻⁵ m²/s
About 5.6×10⁻³ m²/s
thermal-properties-010.explanation: L = 2.0×10⁻³ m, so L² = 4.0×10⁻⁶ m², and α = 0.1388×4.0×10⁻⁶/0.050 ≈ 1.1×10⁻⁵ m²/s. The time for heat absorbed at the front to diffuse through the thickness and reach the back is proportional to L²/α, so the thermal diffusivity is found from the time for half the temperature rise. About 8.0×10⁻⁵ m²/s forgets to multiply by the factor 0.1388, and about 5.6×10⁻³ m²/s forgets to square the thickness, which does not even have units of m²/s. The thermal conductivity is then found as κ = αρc using a separately measured density and specific heat. Because the time scales with the square of the thickness, thicker samples are used for materials with larger thermal diffusivity to keep the time easy to measure.

thermal-properties-011.question: What is the main cause of solids expanding when heated (thermal expansion)?
choices: The interatomic potential is asymmetric (anharmonic), so as the vibration amplitude grows, the average distance between atoms increases
The interatomic potential is parabolic (harmonic), and both the vibration amplitude and the average interatomic distance grow with temperature
As temperature rises, the atoms themselves become larger
thermal-properties-011.explanation: The interatomic potential has an asymmetric shape: repulsion rises steeply as atoms approach, while on the separating side the attraction weakens gradually. As temperature rises and the vibration amplitude grows, atoms swing farther toward the separating side, so the average interatomic distance, the center of the vibration, increases, and this is thermal expansion. If the potential were parabolic (a harmonic oscillator), the vibration would remain symmetric about the equilibrium position however large the amplitude, so the average distance would not change and no thermal expansion would occur. The size of the atoms themselves (the extent of their electron clouds) hardly changes with temperature. Anharmonicity is also the cause of phonon-phonon scattering, which is connected to thermal conductivity having a finite value.

thermal-properties-012.question: Which ordering of linear thermal expansion coefficients near room temperature, from largest to smallest, is correct?
choices: Tungsten > aluminum > polyethylene
Aluminum > polyethylene > tungsten
Polyethylene > aluminum > tungsten
thermal-properties-012.explanation: Near room temperature, the linear thermal expansion coefficient is about 100–200×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for polyethylene, about 23×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for aluminum and about 4.5×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ for tungsten. Materials with stronger interatomic bonds and deeper potential wells tend to show a smaller increase in interatomic distance from vibration at a given temperature, a higher melting point and a smaller linear expansion coefficient. Tungsten, with a melting point above 3400°C, has the smallest value, and polymers, whose molecular chains are held together by weak van der Waals forces, have the largest. For this reason, parts that combine metals with polymers or ceramics develop thermal stress and warping from the difference in expansion when the temperature changes.

thermal-properties-013.question: Which statement correctly explains why the linear thermal expansion coefficient of Fe-36%Ni alloy (Invar) is very small near room temperature, about 1×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹?
choices: Ni suppresses the lattice vibrations of Fe and raises the Debye temperature greatly, so at room temperature the atoms hardly vibrate
Below the Curie temperature, the magnetic volume expansion shrinks as magnetization weakens on heating, canceling normal expansion
On heating, a gradual transformation from BCC to the more densely packed FCC phase proceeds, and the resulting shrinkage cancels the expansion
thermal-properties-013.explanation: Invar is a ferromagnet with a large magnetovolume effect (spontaneous volume magnetostriction), in which spontaneous magnetization lengthens the interatomic distance and enlarges the volume. As temperature rises, the magnetization weakens, so this magnetic expansion decreases and nearly cancels the ordinary thermal expansion from lattice vibration. As a result, the linear expansion coefficient is as small as about 1×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ below the Curie temperature, and Invar is used in precision measuring instruments, containers for liquefied natural gas and the like. Above the Curie temperature the cancellation disappears and it expands like an ordinary metal. Invar is single-phase FCC at room temperature; atomic vibration grows with temperature as usual, and no phase transformation that offsets the expansion takes place.

thermal-properties-014.question: According to the Grüneisen relation, the volume expansion coefficient of a solid is roughly proportional to its constant-volume heat capacity. Which statement correctly describes the linear expansion coefficient of an insulator at low temperatures near absolute zero?
choices: It keeps nearly the same value as at room temperature even as the temperature falls
It grows as the temperature falls and is largest at absolute zero
It decreases with temperature just as the heat capacity does, approaching 0 at absolute zero
thermal-properties-014.explanation: By the Grüneisen relation β = γC_v/(BV) (β is the volume expansion coefficient, γ the Grüneisen parameter, C_v the constant-volume molar heat capacity, B the bulk modulus and V the molar volume), the thermal expansion coefficient follows nearly the same temperature dependence as the heat capacity. At temperatures well below the Debye temperature the heat capacity shrinks in proportion to T³, so the linear expansion coefficient of an insulator also approaches 0 in proportion to T³. Thermal expansion arises from the anharmonicity of vibrations, so at very low temperatures, where vibrations are hardly excited, expansion also hardly occurs. Using the room-temperature value all the way down to very low temperatures greatly overestimates the shrinkage on cooling. Above the Debye temperature the heat capacity is nearly constant, so the linear expansion coefficient is also nearly constant.

thermal-properties-015.question: Red-hot quartz glass (fused silica) rarely cracks when dropped into water, whereas soda-lime glass cracks easily. What is the main reason for the high thermal shock resistance of quartz glass?
choices: Its linear expansion coefficient is very small, about 0.5×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹, so the thermal stress from a temperature difference is small
Its thermal conductivity is as high as a metal's, so the surface–interior temperature difference vanishes quickly
Its fracture toughness is as high as a metal's, so even if thermal stress starts surface cracks they hardly grow
thermal-properties-015.explanation: On quenching, only the surface tries to contract first and is held back by the interior, creating a tensile thermal stress σ ≈ EαΔT/(1 − ν) at the surface. The linear expansion coefficient of quartz glass is about 0.5×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹, only about one twentieth of the roughly 9×10⁻⁶ K⁻¹ of soda-lime glass, so the thermal stress is far smaller for the same temperature difference and it does not crack. The thermal conductivity of quartz glass is low, about 1.4 W/(m·K), and its fracture toughness of about 0.8 MPa·√m is on par with soda-lime glass, both far below metals. Thermal conductivity acts through how the temperature difference between surface and interior develops; under mild heat transfer, materials with higher thermal conductivity are more resistant to thermal shock.

thermal-properties-016.question: The low-temperature heat capacity of a metal can be written C = γT + βT³, where γT is the contribution of conduction electrons and βT³ that of lattice vibrations. Taking γ = 0.695 mJ/(mol·K²) and β = 0.048 mJ/(mol·K⁴) for copper, which is closest to the temperature at which the two contributions are equal?
choices: About 14 K
About 3.8 K
About 2.4 K
thermal-properties-016.explanation: Setting γT = βT³ gives T² = γ/β = 0.695/0.048 ≈ 14.5, so T = √14.5 ≈ 3.8 K. Below this temperature the electronic heat capacity, proportional to T, is larger; above it the lattice heat capacity, proportional to T³, dominates. About 14 K takes γ/β itself as the temperature without the square root, and about 2.4 K takes the cube root. The electronic heat capacity is small because only electrons within about kT of the Fermi level are thermally excited; at room temperature it is only about 1% of the lattice heat capacity (about 3R). Experimentally, C/T plotted against T² gives a straight line whose intercept is γ and whose slope is β. γ is a clue to the electronic density of states at the Fermi level.

thermal-properties-017.question: A furnace wall consists of two layers: inner firebrick (thickness 0.20 m, thermal conductivity 1.0 W/(m·K)) and outer insulating brick (thickness 0.10 m, thermal conductivity 0.20 W/(m·K)). With a temperature difference of 1000 K between the inner and outer faces, which is closest to the steady-state heat flux through the wall? Ignore contact resistance between the layers.
choices: About 7.0 kW/m²
About 2.0 kW/m²
About 1.4 kW/m²
thermal-properties-017.explanation: For layers stacked in series, the thermal resistances per unit area, L/κ, are added. The firebrick gives 0.20/1.0 = 0.20 m²·K/W and the insulating brick 0.10/0.20 = 0.50 m²·K/W, a total of 0.70 m²·K/W, so the heat flux is 1000/0.70 ≈ 1.4×10³ W/m², or about 1.4 kW/m². About 7.0 kW/m² adds κ/L for each layer instead of the resistances, the approach for layers arranged in parallel. About 2.0 kW/m² considers only the insulating brick layer. The temperature drop in each layer is proportional to its resistance, about 290 K across the firebrick and about 710 K across the insulating brick. One also checks that the interface temperature does not exceed the insulating brick's service temperature.

thermal-properties-018.question: Silica aerogel, a porous solid with pores a few tens of nm or smaller, can have a room-temperature thermal conductivity of about 0.015 W/(m·K), lower than that of still air (about 0.025 W/(m·K)). Which is the main reason?
choices: The pores are no larger than the mean free path of air (about 70 nm), suppressing gas conduction, and the solid skeleton is thin
Silica itself conducts heat far less than air, so the larger the fraction of solid skeleton, the lower the overall thermal conductivity becomes
Air in the pores carries heat outward by convection, lowering the surface temperature
thermal-properties-018.explanation: Heat transport in a porous solid is the sum of conduction through the solid skeleton, conduction through the gas in the pores, convection and radiation. Most of an aerogel's volume is pores, and its solid silica skeleton is a network of thin, linked particles, so little heat passes through the solid. Moreover, when the pores are no larger than the mean free path of air (about 70 nm at atmospheric pressure), gas molecules hit the pore walls before colliding with each other, so heat transfer by the gas becomes smaller than in still air (the Knudsen effect). As a whole, a thermal conductivity lower than that of air is obtained. Solid silica has a thermal conductivity of about 1.4 W/(m·K), far higher than air's, so adding more solid raises the conductivity. Convection hardly occurs in such fine pores.

thermal-properties-019.question: For many metals, the measured molar heat capacity at constant pressure, Cp, gradually exceeds the Dulong–Petit value 3R at high temperature. Which is the correct reason?
choices: At high temperature the vibrational degrees of freedom per atom increase from 3 to 6, so the heat capacity keeps rising toward double the value, 6R
The difference Cp − Cv = TVβ²B (β is the volume expansion coefficient, B the bulk modulus) grows with temperature, and electrons also contribute
At high temperature lattice vibrations freeze out, so the heat capacity ought to fall steadily with temperature, but measurement error makes it appear to rise
thermal-properties-019.explanation: 3R is the high-temperature value of the constant-volume heat capacity Cv of a crystal treated as a set of harmonic oscillators. What is readily measured is Cp at constant pressure, and thermodynamics gives Cp − Cv = TVβ²B, so as long as there is thermal expansion Cp exceeds Cv, by an amount that grows with temperature. Contributions from vibrational anharmonicity, the electronic heat capacity proportional to temperature, and vacancy formation at high temperature are added as well, so at high temperature it is not unusual for Cp to exceed 3R by 10% or more. The vibrational freedom is three directions per atom, each with kinetic and potential energy, which is why the value is 3R; it does not rise toward 6R at high temperature. Freezing out of lattice vibrations, which lowers the heat capacity, happens on the low-temperature side.

thermal-properties-020.question: Even when a semiconductor device and a metal heat sink, both polished, are pressed together, a large temperature difference often arises at the contact. Which correctly pairs the main cause of this thermal contact resistance with a countermeasure?
choices: Electrons gather at the contact and reflect heat back; polish the surfaces further to a mirror finish to reduce electron scattering
At the contact, the thermal expansions of the two materials cancel and stop the heat; combine only materials with equal expansion coefficients
Only some surface asperities actually touch, and low-conductivity air remains in the gaps; fill the gaps with thermally conductive grease or pads
thermal-properties-020.explanation: Even polished surfaces have tiny irregularities, and when pressed together only a very small fraction, the asperity tips, actually touch. Heat passes mainly through these narrow contact spots, so the flow is constricted and resistance arises. The remaining gaps are filled with air, whose thermal conductivity is only about 0.025 W/(m·K), so they transmit almost no heat. The gaps are therefore filled with thermal interface materials such as greases, pads or solders containing conductive particles, and the contact pressure is raised to increase the contact area. Because thermal interface materials conduct less well than metals, they should be applied as thinly as possible. The idea that electrons reflect heat has no basis, and differential thermal expansion can cause thermal stress or gaps but is not a mechanism that stops heat flow.

thermal-properties-021.question: In differential scanning calorimetry (DSC), a 10.0 mg sample is heated at 10 K/min, and the heat flow into the sample (the difference from an empty pan) is 1.50 mW. In a temperature range with no transitions, what is the specific heat of the sample?
choices: About 0.90 J/(g·K)
About 0.015 J/(g·K)
About 900 J/(g·K)
thermal-properties-021.explanation: Converting the heating rate to seconds gives 10/60 ≈ 0.167 K/s. The specific heat is the heat flow divided by the sample mass and the heating rate, c = 1.50×10⁻³ W/(0.0100 g × 0.167 K/s) ≈ 0.90 J/(g·K). About 0.015 J/(g·K) divides by the heating rate left as 10 per minute. About 900 J/(g·K) takes the 900 J/(kg·K) obtained with the mass in kg and mistakes it for a per-gram value. In practice the absolute heat flow is prone to instrumental error, so a sapphire standard of known specific heat is often measured under the same conditions and the specific heat is found from the ratio of the heat flows. Where a transition such as melting occurs, the heat of the transition adds to the heat flow, so the specific heat cannot be read directly this way.

thermal-properties-022.question: In isotopically enriched single-crystal diamond, in which the ¹³C fraction is reduced from the natural value of about 1.1% to around 0.1%, the room-temperature thermal conductivity is several tens of percent higher than in natural diamond. What is the main reason?
choices: ¹²C bonds more strongly than ¹³C, so the Young's modulus and sound velocity of the crystal increase and phonons carry heat faster
Randomly mixed atoms of different mass disturb lattice periodicity and scatter phonons; with less of this, the phonon mean free path grows
The nuclear spin of ¹³C nuclei interacts with electrons and absorbs heat, so with less ¹³C less heat is absorbed in the crystal
thermal-properties-022.explanation: Isotopes have the same number of electrons, so interatomic bond strength hardly changes, but the atoms differ in mass. Atoms of different mass mixed at random in the lattice disturb its periodicity as far as phonons are concerned and scatter phonons in the same way as point defects. This scattering is stronger for higher-frequency phonons, and in a crystal such as diamond, with few defects and weak phonon-phonon scattering, it accounts for a noticeable part of the thermal resistance. Reducing ¹³C cuts this scattering, lengthens the phonon mean free path and raises the room-temperature thermal conductivity. Conversely, in alloys with a large mass difference, such as SiGe made by mixing silicon and germanium, this scattering lowers the thermal conductivity greatly, which is exploited in thermoelectric materials.

thermal-properties-023.question: Zirconium tungstate, ZrW₂O₈, contracts isotropically on heating (negative thermal expansion) over a wide temperature range from near 0 K to about 1000 K. What is the main mechanism of this negative thermal expansion?
choices: Linking oxygens vibrating perpendicular to their bonds pull the metal atoms on either side together, so it contracts as these vibrations grow on heating
The interatomic potential is asymmetric the other way round, rising steeply on the stretched side rather than the compressed side, so the average distance shrinks as amplitude grows
Ferromagnetic order is lost on heating and the magnetic contribution to volume decreases, so the whole volume shrinks by the same mechanism as in Invar
thermal-properties-023.explanation: In ZrW₂O₈, ZrO₆ octahedra and WO₄ tetrahedra are linked by sharing corner oxygens. These polyhedra are stiff, and the Zr-O and W-O bond lengths increase slightly on heating, but when a linking oxygen vibrates perpendicular to the Zr-O-W line, the metal atoms on either side are pulled together and their distance shrinks. These transverse vibrations are low in energy, are excited from low temperatures and grow with temperature, so they outweigh the stretching of the bonds themselves and the whole crystal contracts. This is described in terms of rigid-unit modes, vibrations in which the polyhedra rotate with almost no change of shape. The asymmetry of the interatomic potential, the cause of ordinary thermal expansion, acts in the direction of expansion. ZrW₂O₈ is not magnetic, so the Invar mechanism does not apply.

thermal-properties-024.question: Ordinary molded polyethylene has a low thermal conductivity of about 0.4 W/(m·K), but fibers of ultrahigh-molecular-weight polyethylene, whose chains are highly aligned along the fiber, can exceed 10 W/(m·K) along the fiber axis. What is the main reason?
choices: Forming a fiber creates conduction electrons in the regularly aligned chains, so electrons carry heat as they do in a metal
Phonons travel along the strong covalent bonds of the chains with less scattering in amorphous regions, so heat moves quickly along the chains
Drawing greatly increases the density, making the heat capacity per volume tens of times larger, so the thermal conductivity rises in proportion
thermal-properties-024.explanation: The carbon atoms within a polyethylene chain are linked by strong covalent bonds, so phonons travel fast along the chain direction. In ordinary molded parts the chains are folded and entangled in random orientations, phonons are strongly scattered at boundaries between crystalline and amorphous regions and at chain ends, and the chains are joined to one another only by weak intermolecular forces, so the thermal conductivity is low. In highly drawn fibers the chains align along the fiber and the crystallinity rises, so heat is carried quickly along the fiber. Perpendicular to the fiber, heat must pass through the weak bonds between chains, so the conductivity stays low and is strongly anisotropic. Polyethylene remains an electrical insulator even as a fiber, and the change in density on drawing is small.

thermal-properties-025.question: A dense ceramic of thermal conductivity κs contains dispersed, closed spherical pores that can be treated as non-conducting. Using the Maxwell–Eucken equation κ = κs·2(1 − P)/(2 + P), where P is the porosity, about how many times κs is the thermal conductivity of a sintered body with 20% porosity?
choices: About 0.80 times
About 0.36 times
About 0.73 times
thermal-properties-025.explanation: Substituting P = 0.20 gives κ/κs = 2 × 0.80/2.20 = 1.60/2.20 ≈ 0.73, about 0.73 times. About 0.80 times is the rule of mixtures 1 − P for solid and pores arranged parallel to the heat flow; it ignores the fact that heat must detour around the pores and so overestimates the conductivity. About 0.36 times drops the 2 in the numerator and uses (1 − P)/(2 + P). Pores lower the thermal conductivity by more than their volume fraction, but while they are closed, spherical and dispersed, this equation describes them well. When pores become more numerous and interconnected, or flattened so that they block the heat flow, the conductivity falls further. At high temperature, heat transfer by radiation across the pores must also be considered.
